justification: Fresh read, then checked against round 1. This is now clearly ahead of both practical top-ranking pages (GeeksforGeeks, freeCodeCamp) and covers ground Wikipedia has but the practical pages lack (little-o, the two Omega conventions) while Wikipedia in turn has nothing runnable or measured. Nearly every round-1 finding is genuinely fixed, not just gestured at: docs/crosslinks/complexity/big-o-notation.md now exists and is sensible (eight planned links with location and rationale, boundaries-with-siblings section to avoid near-duplicate coverage); the closing paragraph now names what is deliberately left open (recurrences/Master theorem, the wider sorting toolbox) instead of ending inside an exercise solution; the sort code that was printed three times is now printed twice, and the second copy (HybridSort with a cutoff parameter and lo/hi ranges) is a materially different program serving the cutoff exercise, not a padding repeat; the 80,000-lap row is now inside the doubling program so that claim is reproducible; the opening paragraph now states a plain definition of Big-O in its own sentence, addressing the search-intent-landing concern; the growth-rate table's 'O(log n) gains one step' now says '(log base 2)' and the O(n!) row is backed by a precise closed-form note instead of 'grows faster still'; the constants explanation for the sort crossover now names the concrete mechanism (one buffer allocation per MergeSort call, full-depth recursion to n=8 giving 7 recursive calls and 7 merges) instead of asserting it. I re-verified the 7-recursive-calls/7-merge-steps count by hand (Split(0,8) recurses to 1+2+4 = 7 internal merging calls for a power-of-two n=8) and it is correct; web searches for it and for the n! closed-form phrasing found no source match, consistent with original writing, not copy. Measured numbers throughout read as honest and machine-specific: ranges from repeated runs are given rather than single suspiciously-clean numbers ('Three runs gave 7 to 11 ms...', 'Two runs... put the List column at about 12 to 14, 50 to 68...'), noise is called out where it is largest (the 7 ms row, the HashSet microsecond-scale readings), and the toolchain (.NET 10 SDK 10.0.401, runtime 10.0.12, i7-11700K) is stated once, in prose, where measurements start, not as a stamped opening sentence. No filler intro/outro, no boilerplate headings, exercise forms vary (produce-a-witness, extend-the-code-with-a-cutoff, true/false/not-a-claim, a nested-loop trap), and predict-the-output style questions do not leak their output panel above the collapsed solution. What keeps this at 9.0 rather than a flawless 10: (1) the new paragraph on Omega's two literature conventions (the stronger 'every sufficiently large n' form used throughout vs. an 'infinitely many n' form from analytic number theory) is a genuinely non-obvious claim with no source in the front matter backing it, which is the one substantive sourcing gap rule 3 would still flag; (2) the no-Optimize=false crossover run (paragraph beginning 'Now remove the first line of the program and run it again') is still described in prose only, with no accompanying code block or [...]-wildcarded output block that node tools/run-code.mjs actually exercises, so while the transformation is trivial to reproduce by hand, the page itself does not make that specific run checkable the way every other measurement on the page is. Neither is a policy risk and neither reads as padding, filler or fabrication; both are narrow, fixable sourcing/verifiability gaps in an otherwise original, well-measured, honestly-hedged page.

issues.location: "O, Ω and Θ: upper bound, lower bound, both", paragraph beginning "The NIST entry notes that Big-O is often misused...", the sentence on Ω's two conventions in "the wider literature"
issues.problem: The claim that Ω has an older, weaker 'infinitely many n' convention from analytic number theory, versus the NIST/CLRS 'every sufficiently large n' convention used throughout the page, is a non-obvious factual claim (most readers will not know this exists) with no citation, and no source for it appears in the front matter. Wikipedia states the same distinction (Hardy-Littlewood vs. Knuth) but Wikipedia is explicitly excluded as a source by the brief, so it cannot be the citation added here.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite a primary source for the dual convention, e.g. Knuth's own note on the choice of Ω (D. E. Knuth, 'Big Omicron and Big Omega and Big Theta', SIGACT News, 1976) or a textbook passage that discusses it, add it to front matter sources with an accessed date, and cite it inline at that sentence. If no admissible primary source can be found, soften the claim to something the article can support from CLRS/NIST alone (for example, drop the analytic-number-theory aside and just note that some texts require the bound only infinitely often, without naming the convention as an established alternative).
